https://www.thetimes.com/culture/tv-radi.title: The War Against the BBC by Patrick Barwise and Peter York, review — what’s next for the nation’s biggest broadcaster?
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/tv-radi.text:
Timing is the secret of success in all things, which makes this thrice-delayed book either the best book about the BBC yet published — or the worst. The BBC has never been a hotter topic. In an era of global medical crisis and fake news, the corporation is an indispensable information and entertainment service, its supporters say. Over the past nine months audiences for its news bulletins have broken records. And how could the nation have coped during lockdown without Gardeners’ Question Time, Normal People and BBC Bitesize for children?
At the same time its critics have never felt more emboldened. After his election victory Boris Johnson, aided by BBC basher-in-chief Dominic Cummings, began taking on Auntie. They boycotted news programmes they considered hostile and pledged to decriminalise non-payment of the £157.50 licence fee as a prelude to scrapping it altogether.
When Patrick Barwise and Peter York pressed Send on their manuscript in August, after delaying it first for last year’s snap general election, again when Covid-19 hit and a third time when Lord (Tony) quit as BBC director-general, they must have cracked open the champagne and started counting the royalties.
In just a few weeks, though, things have changed. A lot. The BBC is under different management. Tim Davie, Hall’s successor, has set about addressing many of the issues this book raises. He is threatening to sack journalists who breach its strict impartiality rules, and is streamlining management and weeding out “woke” culture and political correctness. After criticism that the corporation favours metropolitan southern audiences over northern and rural ones, he has recommitted the BBC to “universality” — serving all viewers and listeners.
Cummings has departed Downing Street. Lee Cain, his close ally and former No 10 director of communications, preceded him, after a bare-knuckle fight with the former BBC journalist Allegra Stratton, the prime minister’s new official spokeswoman. The moves have prompted speculation that Johnson’s enthusiasm for reforming the corporation will wane.
In the time it has taken to print this book, a truce may have been called in the “war against the BBC” — Martin Bashir’s future excepted — but that’s no reason not to read it. Indeed it’s a “must” for anyone interested in the future of what many regard as Britain’s most important cultural institution and our greatest source of “soft power” on the world stage.
Barwise, emeritus professor of management and marketing at London Business School, and York, a cultural commentator who has read Britain’s cultural trade winds better than most over the past 25 years, provide the most comprehensive modern history of the corporation, analysis of its present predicament and road map for the future. They get to the nub of the sneaking feeling many Brits have: that they love what the BBC stands for, but not how it stands up for it. Most people enjoy the country coming together to sing Rule, Britannia! at the Last Night of the Proms, so why try to ban it to appeal to “the nation as a whole”?
The authors list the market challenges the corporation faces: the rise of deep-pocketed US streaming giants, notably Netflix, Apple and Disney; the increase in the cost of making programmes; 30 per cent funding cuts in real terms since 2010; and the rise of new rivals in the UK, including Times Radio and GB News, a new right-leaning rolling news channel led by Andrew Neil, whom the BBC somehow let slip. They set out the political campaign against the corporation and seek to debunk its critics’ claims as “a mishmash of exaggerations, half-truths, myths and lies”.
They do a good job. I did not know that the BBC’s central role in the UK’s broadcasting ecology means that, according to Deloitte, its gross added value — the standard measurement of an organisation’s economic contribution — is £8.3 billion. That means it “generates about £2 of economic value for every pound of the licence fee”.
The book is best when it begins to map a possible future for the corporation — which Davie is having to do as the BBC gears up for its 100th anniversary in 2022, which coincides with the next round of licence-fee negotiations. Many younger consumers are not buying televisions, which means the licence fee — which is leavied on households with a TV and provides the bulk of the BBC’s £5 billion-a-year income — is becoming hard to justify. But what should replace it?
Barwise and York reject the subscription model touted by some free marketeers, pointing out that, unless the subscription were much higher than the licence fee, it would not raise enough to run the broadcaster. Advertising is out too, because it would severely damage commercial broadcasters, frustrate viewers and listeners, and corrupt the BBC’s mission. A move to fund the corporation out of general taxation would put its income too much at the mercy of politicians.
In the end they plump for a household levy, similar to that to be adopted in Ireland for its national broadcaster, RTE, from 2024. The levy would be set by an independent body, as happens in Germany.
Could Johnson or Sir Keir Starmer be persuaded? Could it mark a permanent truce in the war for the BBC? So much will change after Cummings and after Covid, it’s not impossible.
The War Against the BBC: How an Unprecedented Combination of Hostile Forces Is Destroying Britain’s Greatest Cultural Institution... And Why You Should Care by Patrick Barwise and Peter York Penguin £9.99 pp510

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.title: John Gilbert Getty, heir to oil magnate’s billions, found dead in Texas hotel room
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.text:
John Gilbert Getty, grandson of the oil magnate J Paul Getty and an heir to his multibillion-dollar fortune, has died.
Mr Getty, 52, was found unresponsive in a hotel room in San Antonio, Texas, the website TMZ reported. It said that police did not suspect foul play.
A spokesman for Gordon Getty, his father, said: “With a heavy heart, Gordon Getty announces the death of his son, John Gilbert Getty. John was a talented musician who loved rock and roll. He will be deeply missed.”
The 86-year-old father is a classical musician and philanthropist, the fourth and only surviving one of J Paul Getty’s five sons by four of his five wives.
John Gilbert’s death is one of several recent deaths in the family. His mother, Ann Getty, a prominent philanthropist, died of a heart attack, aged 79, in September, and his older brother Andrew died of an intestinal ulcer in 2015 at the age of 47. He had toxic levels of methamphetamine in his system.
John Gilbert is survived by his brothers Peter and Billy and his daughter Ivy, as well as three half-sisters his father had with a mistress. They came to public attention in 1999 when their mother, Cynthia Beck, sought the right in court for them to use the Getty surname.
“My father was awesome,” Ivy, 26, wrote on Instagram. “Coolest man to ever land on this planet and I will forever be the proudest daughter. Love you so much Dad . . . life is cruel sometimes . . . I have not one, but two guardian angels watching over me now.”
John Gilbert’s grandfather, J Paul Getty, died in 1976. He merged several smaller oil companies to form Getty Oil before striking deals with Saudi Arabia.
For a time he was the richest man in the world. A passionate art collector, he left most of his estate to the Getty Museum, an art museum in Los Angeles. His large family inherited billions through a trust with interests in Getty Oil, which was sold to Texaco in the late 1980s.
A Forbes magazine profile in 2014, which estimated the family’s modern-day wealth at $5 billion, said that “the story of the famed Getty family is one of the most obvious examples that money, cold hard cash, doesn’t buy happiness”.
John Paul Getty III, John Gilbert’s cousin and another grandson of J Paul, was kidnapped by Italian gangsters in Rome in 1973, when he was 16. His grandfather refused to pay the ransom of $17 million, arguing that to do so would make his other grandchildren jealous. The ransom was eventually paid when his captors cut off the boy’s ear and posted it to a newspaper. After his kidnapping he battled with drug and alcohol addiction. He suffered a stroke in 1981, which left him quadriplegic, partially blind and unable to speak. He died aged 54 in 2011.
His stepmother, Talitha Pol, an actress, had died of a heroin overdose in 1971.
Timothy Getty, the oil magnate’s youngest son, was diagnosed with a brain tumour at the age of six and died aged 12 in 1958.
The eldest son, George Getty, died in mysterious circumstances aged 49 in 1973. Many believe that his death was a suicide.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/healthcare/a.title: Battlefield guides plant poppy crosses at soldiers’ graves
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/healthcare/a.text:
Ahead of Armistice Day each year a flood of relatives and military historians make their pilgrimage to the battlefield cemeteries of the First World War to plant a poppy cross and remember the ultimate sacrifice made by millions of young men.
This year battlefield guides with no tours to lead thanks to lockdown restrictions across Europe have stepped in to pay their respects at gravestones for those stuck at home under lockdown.
One of the graves that has received a poppy cross is for Lieutenant Harry Renton, of the 9th (Service) Battalion, The King’s Royal Rifle Corps, whose final resting place was only identified this year and whose dedication ceremony was cancelled by Covid-19.
The body of Lieutenant Renton, who was only 20 when he was killed near Hooge, Belgium, on July 20, 1915, had been discovered in 1926 and buried at Oosttaverne Wood Cemetery with a marker declaring him to be an “Unknown Lieutenant”.
A head of house at Harrow school, he kept wicket in the Eton and Harrow match at Lords in 1914 and was to have entered Oxford University in October 1914, but on the outbreak of the war he joined the Army.
Genevra Charsley, who runs the Flanders Battlefield Tour company with her fiancé Jacques Ryckebosch, placed a cross at Lieutenant Renton’s new gravestone this week on behalf of Andrew Thornton, the historian who discovered his resting place.
She also read aloud the exhortation, which begins, “They shall grow not old, as we that are left grow old”, in place of the dedication ceremony that could not happen.
Mr Thornton said: “I asked Gen to do it on my behalf. It is just a little gesture really to show in remembrance. This was the first year he has had a known grave and I know it means a lot to his family.”
Ms Charsley made the offer on social media to place poppy crosses in cemeteries for anyone unable to make the journey this year and over two days has covered 250km to help 60 people to commemorate fallen soldiers.
“It’s just a simple act, but it matters to people,” she said.
“Where people have sent me photographs and images of the soldiers I have printed them out and stuck them to the top of the poppy cross, so when we have placed it at the graves people walking by can see them.”
She has been contacted by families as well as schools, who have been teaching their children about former pupils who were killed during the war.
The past year has been hard for battlefield tour guides, who are almost all freelance workers, as well as for the accommodation and hospitality businesses that service the thousands of Britons who make the journey to Flanders to retrace the steps of ancestors and pay their respects as the cemeteries that dot the now peaceful landscape.
“We would normally be out six days a week with two vehicles doing tours,” Ms Charlsey said.
“Since mid-March we have done about ten tours in total. It’s been a testing year and I think there are probably a few more testing months to come.
“But when I think I have gone through anything bad then I look at the graves and remind myself they went through much worse and it puts it in perspective.”
This year the Last Post ceremony on Armistice Day at the Menin Gate, in Ypres, will have no parade and no crowds because of the lockdown restrictions in force in Belgium.
